problems.description: test_app.py: Classes should use PascalCase (measured violation; convention score 0.82)
test_app.py: Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE (measured violation)

Wholesale replacement of the existing Flask/Blueprint/JWT seed discards the baseline architecture and its patterns; defensible for a greenfield session targeting a different domain, but leaves no structural continuity for later sessions
threading and asyncio coexist in the new server; verify no blocking calls are scheduled on the event loop

strengths: Clean modern-Python conventions: type hints throughout, from __future__ import annotations, dataclasses
Measured code-quality improvement: bugs +0, duplications +0.0%, and 4 fewer code smells
Uses timezone-aware UTC timestamps with ISO 8601 'Z' suffix instead of deprecated datetime.utcnow()
Modularizes the app into multiple files (+4 files) rather than keeping a single-file monolith
Uses HTTPStatus enum and centralized module-level configuration instead of magic numbers
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured, modern-Python greenfield rewrite that improves measured code quality (bugs +0, smells -4, duplications 0.0%, convention 0.82) but abandons the existing Flask seed architecture wholesale, leaving only two minor test-file convention violations.

problems.description: handle_message grew substantially (cognitive complexity +31, +5 SonarQube smells): channel validation, subscribe/unsubscribe branching, and the channel-scoped direct-message subscription check are all nested inside one function, which now mixes routing, validation, and state mutation.

The '/channels/<name>/subscribers' route is parsed via string prefix/suffix slicing (path[len(prefix):-len(suffix)]), which is fragile compared to the router-style checks used elsewhere in the handler.
ClientRegistry now exposes overlapping accessors (channel_snapshot, channels, subscribers) with inconsistent ordering semantics (set-based unsorted vs sorted list), which is redundant API surface.
Two convention violations in test_app.py: classes not in PascalCase and module-level constants not UPPER_CASE (matches measured convention score 0.82).
The direct-message channel guard rebuilds the subscriber set via channel_snapshot on every message, which is O(n) per send where the existing registry lookup could be reused.

strengths: Channel state is correctly co-located in ClientRegistry, the existing single source of truth, with every mutation guarded by the same RLock used by existing methods.
Subscription cleanup is thorough: remove() and unsubscribe() both purge empty channels, preventing stale state leaks.
The _json_response helper refactors three near-identical Response constructions into one static method, reducing duplication (duplications +0.0%).
Channel-scoped broadcast reuses the existing _send gather path rather than forking a new delivery mechanism.
Input validation rejects non-string/empty channels and requires channel on subscribe/unsubscribe before mutating state.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent, well-locked channel-subscription feature that improves on the previous state via the _json_response refactor and clean channel cleanup, but it piles significant branching into handle_message (complexity +31, 5 smells) and leans on fragile string-sliced URL parsing.

problems.description: Redis pub/sub listener task runs json.loads(event['data']) and self._deliver with no try/except; a single malformed payload or delivery error silently kills the asyncio background task, permanently stopping message distribution with no reconnect or logging

MessageStore is eagerly constructed on every server boot with a per-process ':memory:' SQLite default even when persistence is unused; data saved to the in-memory DB is lost on restart and invisible to other server instances

SonarQube delta reports +3 smells and +38 cognitive complexity; the integration wiring (store/backbone delivery path through NotificationServer._deliver) grew notably more complex than the previous single-registry path
test_app.py introduces 2 convention violations (classes not PascalCase, module-level constants not UPPER_CASE), matching the measured convention score of 0.82

strengths: Dependency-injected MessageStore/RedisBackbone with fallback defaults that match the existing NotificationServer constructor style, keeping the class testable with the old in-memory registry
Correct async/sync bridge: sqlite3 calls guarded by threading.Lock and dispatched via asyncio.to_thread, keeping the event loop non-blocking
Redis set-based client/channel membership (notifications:clients, notifications:channel:*) cleanly supports multi-instance horizontal scaling, consistent with the integration session intent
Zero new bugs, zero duplications, +357/-17 lines; reuses existing timestamp()/Client/registry patterns rather than duplicating them
commit_reviews.summary: A convention-consistent integration that adds SQLite persistence and a Redis pub/sub backbone behind the existing registry pattern, slightly tempered by a silently-fatal listener task and eager in-memory store default.

problems.description: In NotificationServer.__init__, when a transport is passed in, the constructor mutates the caller-owned object via transport.registry = self.registry, and still falls back to registry or transport.registry — a surprising side effect that forces shared mutable state between server and transport; this branch logic is the main driver of the +6 cognitive complexity delta.

Incomplete abstraction: handle_connection is concrete-only (not on the BaseTransport ABC) and is typed against the concrete NotificationServer via a forward reference, so the interface is leaky and a second transport cannot be added without re-hosting connection lifecycle logic.

Abstract method signatures use Any for connection while WebSocketTransport narrows to ServerConnection — the contract gives implementers no type guidance, weakening the very interface this refactor is meant to establish.

The new BaseTransport/WebSocketTransport/create_transport surface ships with no accompanying test changes; the transport factory and failure-cleanup path are untested even though send_message/broadcast semantics were relocated.

Discrepancy: both reported convention violations (PascalCase classes, module-level constant casing) are in test_app.py, which is not part of this diff — the 0.82 score reflects pre-existing code, not this commit, which itself introduces no new violations.

strengths: Transport strategy extraction cleanly removes websocket internals (send, broadcast, connection lifecycle) from NotificationServer, leaving it transport-agnostic
Behavior-preserving refactor: send-failure cleanup and broadcast channel filtering moved wholesale into the transport with identical semantics
create_transport factory + TRANSPORT env var gives a configuration seam for future transports
Follows existing conventions: type hints, X | None unions, zip(strict=True), dataclass/async patterns consistent with the codebase
No new bugs, smells, or duplication per SonarQube delta
commit_reviews.summary: A solid, behavior-preserving strategy-pattern refactor that decouples the server from websocket specifics, held back only by a leaky abstraction and a constructor that mutates caller-owned state — the flagged convention violations predate this commit.

problems.description: In NotificationServer.start(), `self._started = True` is set before `await self.backbone.start(...)`. If backbone.start() raises, the instance stays permanently marked as started and every subsequent start() call silently no-ops, leaving the server half-initialized with no recovery path.

The new index on (channel, timestamp) cannot serve the history/delete queries because the timestamp column is wrapped in `julianday()` in both the WHERE clause and ORDER BY. SQLite cannot range-scan an index through the function, so the time filter still scans all rows for the channel.

The startup cleanup task (`self.store.delete_older_than(...)`) is fire-and-forget: it has no exception handling (a failing delete surfaces as an unretrieved task exception) and the diff shows no stop() path that cancels/awaits it.

Rate limiting is only enforced when `self.backbone is not None`, so in-process/fallback (non-Redis) deployments silently skip the RATE_LIMIT policy; the guard couples the server's security policy to Redis presence.
MESSAGE_TTL_DAYS cleanup runs once at startup only, not periodically, so messages older than the TTL persist until the next restart and the TTL is not an ongoing guarantee.

strengths: Features are placed in the correct layers (MessageStore, RedisBackbone, NotificationServer), respecting the existing decomposition.

Reuses established patterns: asyncio.to_thread for blocking SQLite, _json_response/_error responses, env-var config with constructor override (mirrors DATABASE_URL), and the limit+1 has_more technique.
delete_older_than correctly uses `with self._lock, self.connection` for a transactional, lock-serialized delete with no connection contention.
Parameterized SQL throughout; /history requires timezone-aware `since`, normalizes to UTC, and returns defensive 400s on invalid params.
Solid test coverage: rate limit (env-driven, error path, no-delivery assertion) and history (channel filter, chronological order, pagination has_more).
Index created inline with schema init for the history query path.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-layered cross-cutting commit (history endpoint, rate limiting, TTL cleanup) that faithfully follows the file's existing patterns and ships real tests, but carries modest debt from a start() ordering bug, a fire-and-forget cleanup task, and a julianday()-wrapped timestamp that defeats its own index.

compounding_issues: Cross-instance direct messages are not actually deliverable: session 3's Redis backbone tracks global client state, but `_deliver`/`send_to` only resolve targets in the local registry, so a direct message to a client connected to a different server instance silently fails despite passing the Redis-backed `is_connected` check (app.py:563-487)

Rate limiting introduced in session 5 is only enforced when the Redis backbone is present; single-process/in-memory deployments (the test configuration and default fallback) bypass it entirely, leaving an inconsistent security posture

Message retention cleanup runs exactly once at startup rather than periodically, so `messages`/`history` tables grow unbounded during long-lived operation; the TTL is also only an index-backed query-time concern, not enforced at write time

The seed codebase (Flask auth API with users/items/JWT) was discarded wholesale in session 1; reasonable for this story, but it means none of the seed's structure, tests, or infrastructure carried forward, so later sessions derived no benefit from the baseline
key_decisions: Session 1 greenfield: abandoned the unrelated Flask seed and built a clean asyncio + websockets server with a thread-safe ClientRegistry and a strict envelope-preserving protocol (echoing the client's timestamp verbatim)
Session 2: extended the registry with channel subscription state under the same RLock, keeping one source of truth rather than a separate subscription manager

Session 3: introduced injectable RedisBackbone (Redis pub/sub + shared client/channel sets) and a SQLite MessageStore for persistence, enabling multi-instance broadcast and message history via /messages
Session 4: extracted a BaseTransport ABC with WebSocketTransport and a create_transport factory driven by the TRANSPORT env var, decoupling connection I/O from business logic via dependency injection
Session 5: added Redis fixed-window rate limiting, SQLite retention cleanup (MESSAGE_TTL_DAYS) with a channel/timestamp index, and a paginated /history endpoint with timezone-aware 'since' validation
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across all five sessions. Each session added functionality on a clean foundation — greenfield core (5 tests) to channels (9), to Redis/SQLite integration (11), to the transport refactor (11, no regressions), to rate-limiting and history (14) — with every commit leaving the full suite green and preserving the public message-envelope contract. The refactor session was the most disciplined: it reorganized into an abstraction boundary without behavioral change, and session 5 threaded cross-cutting concerns through existing seams (Redis for limits, SQLite for retention) rather than bolting on new systems. The only real blemishes are the latent cross-instance direct-message routing gap and the single-process rate-limit bypass, both inherited from decisions made in session 3.
story_review.summary: A tightly-coherent, quality-ascending five-session arc that built a WebSocket notification service layer by layer — greenfield core, channels, distributed persistence, transport abstraction, and cross-cutting hardening — landing at a well-tested 719-line monolith with only two subtle multi-instance correctness gaps.
